titre: Gift and Counter-Gift in Marcel Mauss
accroche: In 1925, a sociologist explains the economy of societies without markets with a single rule: you must always give back what you have received.
contenu_vulgarise:
A Maori chief offers a taonga, a precious object laden with history. There it is, received: polished, respected, impossible to keep for oneself without unease. No law requires it to be given back. And yet almost no one keeps it.

## The Mechanism

In 1925, in the journal *L'Année sociologique*, Marcel Mauss publishes the *Essai sur le don : forme et raison de l'échange dans les sociétés archaïques* (*The Gift: Forms and Functions of Exchange in Archaic Societies*). In it he describes a system of exchange that predates the market, in which the circulation of goods among clans, tribes, or chiefs follows three linked obligations: to give, to receive, to give back. Refusing to give, refusing to receive, or refusing to give back amounts, in these societies, to a declaration of war or a loss of rank.

Mauss builds this thesis on precise ethnographic examples. Among the Maori of New Zealand, the sage Tamati Ranapiri explains to the ethnographer Elsdon Best what the hau is: the force that dwells in taonga and drives whoever holds them to give them back to their original owner, on pain of misfortune. On the northwest coast of America, among the Tlingit and the Haida, the same principle takes a competitive form that Mauss calls potlatch (a term that originally meant “to feed”): rival chiefs distribute and destroy goods in public, each trying to give back more than he received, on pain of social downfall. In the Trobriand Islands, studied by Bronislaw Malinowski, the kula circulates two categories of prestige objects in opposite directions among dozens of islands; they serve only to be exchanged and then given back.

Mauss calls these exchanges a total social fact: a single transaction engages law, religion, economics, kinship, and morality all at once. What 19th-century anthropology described as primitive barter, clumsy and without money, Mauss reads as a system of credit and obligation as rigorous as a contract.

## What It Shifts

The error Mauss corrects is not only ethnographic. It touches on the idea that market exchange, self-interested and free of debt, would be the natural and original form of the human economy, of which so-called archaic societies offered only an imperfect version. Mauss reverses the hierarchy: the obligatory gift comes first, and the anonymous market is the recent historical exception. Published seven years after the armistice of 1918, the essay closes on the idea that entire peoples learned to exchange without exterminating one another, long before any contract imposed it on them. The birthday present we feel bound to return one day, with no law requiring it, is the last vestige.

carte.punch: In 1925, a sociologist explains the economy without markets with a single rule: always give back.
carte.idee: Drawing on the Maori hau and the North American potlatch, Mauss describes a system in which giving creates the obligation to receive and then to give back, with no law imposing it. He sees in it proof that disinterested exchange is not the original form of the human economy, but its recent exception.
carte.source_courte: Mauss, Essai sur le don (The Gift), 1925

quiz.question: Why are the potlatch and the kula of particular interest to Mauss?
choix: Because they prove that societies without writing had no notion of private property
Because they show that a gift can create an obligation as binding as a contract, with no law to impose it
Because they demonstrate that barter preceded money in all known civilizations
Because they reveal the existence of a free, competitive market before European capitalism
quiz.explication: Neither private property, nor a universal prehistory of barter, nor a free market is at stake: Mauss shows that giving commits one to receiving and then to giving back, on pain of social sanction, even though no written law exists.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the word “potlatch,” which Mauss uses for the competition of gifts among the Tlingit and the Haida, originally mean?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that “potlatch” originally meant “to feed,” before coming to designate this competition of gifts and public destruction.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Mauss, what does someone risk who refuses to give, to receive, or to give back in these societies?
choix: A fine set by a customary court
A declaration of war or a loss of rank
Immediate expulsion from the clan with no recourse
Nothing, since these three obligations are merely customs without consequences
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that refusing to give, to receive, or to give back amounts, in these societies, to a declaration of war or a loss of rank.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which Maori explains to the ethnographer Elsdon Best what the hau of the taonga is?
choix: The Tlingit chief cited by Malinowski
Marcel Mauss, during fieldwork he carried out in person
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is the Maori sage Tamati Ranapiri who explains to the ethnographer Elsdon Best the force of the hau that drives people to give back taonga.
